You're missing some subtle distinctions.

Most leglock positions are symmetrical, meaning that your opponent has an opportunity to attack your legs while you are attacking theirs.

A lot of leg attacks require you to abandon top position before you even start attacking. That's contrary to the overall philosophy.

For example, if you achieve a dominant position, then abandon it to dive for a toehold, you're going all-in on that submission. If you have a dominant position and start setting up an armbar, then by the time you give up that position, if you even have to, you've gotten 70% of the way to finishing the submission already and are rarely going to lose it.

So, as I've mentioned before, if we can assume that the consequences of any failed submission are identical, then the submissions you want to attempt are the ones with the highest percentage of success from your position.

There are plenty of places to attack for leglocks that are super advantageous and lead to bettering your position even if you fail, but there are very few dominant positions that fall into that category. You don't often see leg locks from a dominant position or side control, or the back. You see them from inferior or neutral positions.

What this means is that if you specialize in leglocks, you are frequently specializing in working from a disadvantage and trying to turn it into an advantage. Now you have to have a lot higher skill level in that position than your opponent than you would from a more dominant position.

I love leglocks. I'm usually the 'leglock person' at whatever training facility I'm at, but there are distinct disadvantages to them that you need to understand in order to approach using them to their best effect.

By far my most successful method is moving out though. You establish your grip on the inside of the pants at both knees with your same side hands, then go to combat base and stand. Push their knees towards their chest and backstep your trapped foot, then pull their knees and either continue your backstep into side control, or knee sweep to knee on belly.

What you don't want to do is try to pass straight through their knee shield. With a decent frame, the knee shield is VERY hard to smash pass through. However, if they let their knee drift down from your shoulder towards your sternum, you can take a grip on the outside of the knee and stiff-arm it straight down, then donkey kick your trapped leg out and bring it back in. While keeping that knee pinned, you backstep the other leg and drop your shoulder into side control.

There are multiple steps to completing each of these passes, and you aren't going to hit them all the way the first time, obviously. So drill the technique for a few days, then start working the first couple of steps.

Just getting the inside knee grips and going to combat base will change the dynamic of the roll a lot, so that's a good place to start. Measure success by how many steps you execute, not whether you necessarily secured the pass or not. Once you're consistently executing all of the steps, you can move to working on securing the pass, since that's really a different set of skills, just like breaking the guard is different than passing the guard.
